questions.stem: A 2-month-old has tachypnea and poor feeding. Which combination most strongly suggests heart failure from myocardial dysfunction?

options.A: Diaphoresis with feeds, hepatomegaly, and a gallop

questions.rationale: Feeding-related diaphoresis, hepatomegaly, and a gallop are classic infant heart-failure clues.

option_explanations.A: Correct. This combination strongly localizes the problem to the cardiovascular system.

questions.board_pearl: Infant feeding is an exertional stress test; diaphoresis and respiratory distress with feeds can signal heart failure.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old with clinically suspected myocarditis has a mildly elevated troponin that falls over 24 hours, but ventricular function remains depressed. Which interpretation is best?

options.A: The falling troponin does not by itself establish recovery of ventricular function
options.B: The patient is cured because troponin decreased
options.D: The depressed function must be unrelated

questions.rationale: Biomarkers and ventricular function may recover on different timelines; troponin trend alone is not a complete measure of recovery.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Continue to assess function and clinical status.
option_explanations.E: Return to exercise requires broader recovery criteria.

questions.board_pearl: Trend the patient, not just the troponin.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has acute chest pain and elevated troponin. Echo shows normal ventricular function. He has a recent blunt chest injury during sports and no infectious symptoms. Which diagnosis should be considered before assuming myocarditis?
questions.rationale: Recent blunt chest trauma provides a direct alternative cause of myocardial injury and troponin elevation.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Trauma-related myocardial injury fits the context.
option_explanations.B: Age and myocardial injury pattern do not fit.
option_explanations.E: Acute trauma-associated presentation is inconsistent with chronic DCM.

questions.board_pearl: Troponin elevation has a differential; always integrate mechanism and timeline.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with myocarditis and mild pulmonary congestion is stable in the PICU. Which bedside trend is most useful for recognizing early deterioration?

options.A: Serial perfusion, mental status, urine output, blood pressure, and rhythm assessment

questions.rationale: Clinical trajectory in myocarditis depends on hemodynamics and electrical stability, so serial bedside assessment is crucial.

option_explanations.A: Correct. These variables directly reflect cardiac output and rhythm stability.

questions.board_pearl: Myocarditis can change quickly; serial bedside physiology matters as much as any single test.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with chest pain and elevated troponin has preserved EF on echocardiography. Why can CMR still be useful?

options.A: It can detect myocardial edema and injury despite preserved global systolic function

questions.rationale: Myocarditis may produce tissue-level inflammation despite normal global EF; CMR can detect edema and nonischemic injury.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Tissue characterization adds information beyond EF.
option_explanations.E: CMR informs risk but does not guarantee outcome.

questions.board_pearl: Preserved EF does not exclude meaningful myocardial inflammation.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with myocarditis has a brief run of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia on telemetry but is asymptomatic. Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Treat it as evidence of electrical instability and continue close monitored care
options.B: Ignore it because there was no syncope
options.D: Clear for sports because it was nonsustained

questions.rationale: Ventricular tachyarrhythmia in myocarditis is clinically significant even without symptoms and warrants continued monitoring and risk assessment.

option_explanations.B: Absence of symptoms does not make VT benign.

questions.board_pearl: Asymptomatic does not equal low-risk when ventricular tachycardia is documented.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old with suspected myocarditis has no identified infectious agent despite an appropriate evaluation. Which statement is best?

options.A: The diagnosis can remain clinically valid even when no pathogen is identified
options.C: A pathogen must be found before supportive care begins
options.D: The child must have congenital heart disease
options.E: A normal viral panel proves an autoimmune cause

questions.rationale: Many pediatric myocarditis cases remain without a proven pathogen; diagnosis is based on clinical, imaging, laboratory, and sometimes biopsy evidence.

option_explanations.C: Supportive treatment should not wait for pathogen proof.
option_explanations.E: Negative viral testing does not prove autoimmunity.

questions.board_pearl: Etiologic uncertainty is common; do not mistake it for diagnostic invalidity.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old on VA-ECMO for fulminant myocarditis develops progressive LV distention and pulmonary edema. Which advanced-care concept may become relevant?

options.A: Left-heart decompression/unloading may be considered by the mechanical support team

questions.rationale: On VA-ECMO, inadequate LV ejection can lead to left-sided distention and pulmonary edema; specialized teams may use unloading/decompression strategies.

option_explanations.A: Correct. This is an advanced support issue managed by an experienced center.

questions.board_pearl: Mechanical support treats circulation but can create new hemodynamic problems that require expert management.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old recovering from myocarditis has normal EF but persistent exertional dyspnea. What is the best approach?

options.A: Reassess for residual cardiac dysfunction, arrhythmia, or other causes before clearing activity
options.C: Clear for full sports because EF is normal
options.D: Ignore symptoms if troponin is normal

questions.rationale: Persistent exertional symptoms require reassessment because functional recovery may lag or arrhythmia/residual injury may persist despite normalized EF.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Symptoms should be explained before clearance.
option_explanations.B: Deconditioning is possible but should not be presumed.

questions.board_pearl: Persistent symptoms after myocarditis deserve a cardiac explanation before being labeled benign.

questions.stem: Which finding after apparent clinical recovery from myocarditis may justify continued rhythm surveillance?
questions.rationale: Residual scar can provide an arrhythmogenic substrate even after symptoms and function improve.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Scar can matter for long-term electrical risk.

questions.board_pearl: Scar can outlast inflammation and symptoms.
